description: Pong online free: the original arcade duel against the computer. Bounce the ball past the CPU paddle — first to 7 wins the match.
lede: The game that started it all: one ball, two paddles, and a race to 7. You guard the bottom of the table, the computer guards the top, and every rally gets a little faster. Drag your paddle — or steer with the arrow keys — and send the ball where the computer is not.

p: Press Start the match and the ball serves from the centre. Slide your paddle to meet it and bounce it back toward the computer's side. If the ball slips past the computer's paddle, you score; if it slips past yours, the computer scores. The first side to 7 points wins the match.

The ball gets faster with every paddle hit, so rallies start gentle and end frantic. Where the ball strikes your paddle decides where it goes next: hit it with the middle and it flies straight, catch it with the edge and it shoots off at a sharp angle. Use that to aim for the corners the computer cannot reach.
Every rally ends in a point for one side. There are no lives and no second chances — the match is a straight race to 7, and the scoreboard in the middle of the table keeps count the whole way.

sections.h: The first video game anyone played
p: Pong was released by Atari in 1972, and it was the first video game to become a commercial hit. Nolan Bushnell and Allan Alcorn built it as a training exercise — a simple table-tennis game with two paddles and a square ball — and the first prototype, installed in a bar in Sunnyvale, California, earned so many quarters that the coin box jammed within days.

It worked because anyone could understand it in five seconds: move the paddle, hit the ball, do not let it past you. That simplicity turned Pong into the template for the whole arcade era, and it is still the purest rally game you can play — no power-ups, no levels, just you, the ball, and the paddle on the other side.

ol: Stay near the centre when the ball is on the computer's side: from the middle you can reach either corner in time.
Aim with the edge of your paddle. A ball struck near the edge flies off at a steep angle the computer struggles to cover.
Do not chase the ball — move early. Watch where the ball is heading, not where it is now.
When the rally speeds up, make small adjustments. Big sweeping moves overshoot and leave your side of the table open.
The computer drifts back to the centre while the ball heads your way. A sharp-angled shot right after your return catches it out of position.
